title: Rainfall as IV for agricultural loan demand

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
To answer the research question of whether access to credit improves agricultural output, we will employ the Instrumental Variable (IV) approach. The key assumption for this method is that the instrument (annual rainfall deviation from mean) affects the outcome (log crop yield) only through its effect on the treatment (log loans per capita), which is known as the exclusion restriction. Another important assumption is that the instrument is relevant, meaning it has a significant effect on the treatment. The first stage of the IV analysis will examine the relationship between rainfall deviation and credit demand, and the second stage will use the predicted credit demand to estimate its effect on crop yield.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load necessary libraries
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(plm)
library(AER)

# Load the data
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s19_data.csv")

# First stage: regression of x (log loans per capita) on z (rainfall deviation) and controls
first_stage_model <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = data)

# Summary of first stage
summary(first_stage_model)

# Second stage: IV regression using the fitted values from the first stage as instruments
second_stage_model <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls, data = data, 
                            instruments = ~ controls + z)

# Print the results of the second stage
summary(second_stage_model)

# Basic robustness checks: checking for overidentification
overid_test <- overid-test(second_stage_model)
print(overid_test)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect the coefficient on the log loans per capita in the second stage regression to be positive, indicating that an increase in credit demand (as a result of higher rainfall deviation) leads to an improvement in agricultural output (log crop yield). The magnitude of this effect is expected to be moderate, given that credit access can influence farmers' ability to invest in inputs and technologies that enhance productivity, but it's also subject to various factors such as farm size, soil quality, and management practices. The exact magnitude will depend on the data and the strength of the instrument. A significant and positive coefficient would support the hypothesis that access to credit improves agricultural output.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV/2SLS — instrument: rainfall; first stage: rainfall → loans; exclusion restriction: rainfall ⊥ yield | credit
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Credit access significantly increases crop yields
_ground_truth.main_effect: 10% increase in credit → 4% yield increase (IV estimate)
